chunks: "If I had to pick one word, it's capacitive, but I'd add that the better description is a time-varying current sink.
The transistors are CMOS gates, so almost all of the dynamic power goes into charging and discharging capacitance every clock cycle. That's the alpha C V squared f formula.
So there's a lot of switched capacitance in there, plus a lot of on-die decoupling capacitance that helps it. On average you can say it looks resistive. A core at 0.
9 volts pulling 54 amps looks like about 17 milliohms at DC. But that number isn't a real resistor.
If the workload goes idle, the current drops to leakage in microseconds, the voltage hasn't changed, so the 'resistance' just jumped.
It acts like a current source that the software controls. It's not really inductive.
The inductance you see in the power path belongs to the package, the vias and the board, and it sits between the regulator and the chip.
That inductance matters because when current steps by tens of amps in a few nanoseconds, L di over dt gives you droop.
So the regulator and the decoupling network have to treat the SoC as a fast, large current step with a tight voltage tolerance, and design the supply impedance to match that."
